source.title: Exploiting the Index Gradients for Optimization-Based Jailbreaking on Large Language Models
source.authors: Jia-Hui Li; Yongchang Hao; Hao-Yu Xu; Xing Wang; Yu Hong

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or document mismatch. Some table symbols are poorly rendered in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether adversarial suffixes can elicit harmful responses from aligned models, using attack success rates. It evaluates a new optimization procedure and compares it with suffix-attack baselines; it does not test fine-tuning or first-token concentration.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASRs for optimized adversarial suffix attacks on harmful instructions, which bear on V4. It does not test compliant prefilling, decoding changes, or the proposed first-token distribution mechanism. Fine-tuning and other findings mentioned in related work are citations, not this study's results. Table 3's condition symbols are poorly rendered, so its four condition rows cannot be reliably mapped to the presence or absence of harmful guidance and suffix initialization.
record.test_reason: This is an attack-methods paper. It uses GCG-style suffixes, optimised to start with 'Sure, here is…', as a tool. It reports only ASR comparisons between its MAGIC optimiser and other attack methods, plus wall-time and iteration counts. There is no no-suffix refusal baseline and no analysis of whether getting past the opening tokens is what defeats refusal. Every ASR row is the study's own method or a baseline method in a method comparison, so no row tests V4 as a claim about shallow alignment. No other version (fine-tuning, KL, localisation, cause, deepening) is touched; fine-tuning and decoding attacks appear only as citations in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MAGIC (gradient-based index selection plus adaptive multi-coordinate updates) speeds GCG-style suffix optimisation, up to 1.5x, with ASR equal to or above the baselines. They report 74% on Llama2-7B-chat and 54% transfer to GPT-3.5. In the limitations they say transfer may weaken across model families. The claim that it 'works across' closed models should be tempered: closed-model transfer ASRs other than GPT-3.5 are 0–16%.
record.recipe_differences: This is an optimization-based adversarial-suffix attack study, proposing gradient-based index selection and adaptive multi-coordinate updates. It does not reproduce the fine-tuning intervention or first-token KL measurement in the cited original studies.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies by target model and transfer setup (suffix optimized on Vicuna versus Vicuna & Guanaco). Table 3 also varies harmful guidance and suffix initialization, but the condition markers are not recoverable from the supplied text.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimised adversarial suffixes reach 54–100% ASR on four open 7B chat models (AdvBench, single prompt). Transfer to closed models (GPT-3.5/4/4o, Claude-3 Haiku) is mostly 0–16%, with MAGIC's 54% on GPT-3.5 the exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attack-efficacy benchmark for GCG-family suffix optimisers (method performance, not a test of opening-token shallowness)

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. ASR uses refusal-word detection followed by a ChatGPT-3.5 checker and manual review; the authors acknowledge refusal-word detection is imperfect. The text does not clearly preserve Table 3's condition markers.
record.rows_left_out: Other methods in Table 1 and Table 2, including LLM-based baselines, PAIR, MAC, PS, and additional I-GCG transfer results, are omitted to keep within the 60-row limit and prioritize GCG/MAGIC results, zero or low transfer results, and condition-dependent comparisons. Table 3 reports iteration counts and Table 4 reports timing as well as ASR; timing and iteration outcomes do not measure the behaviour named by V4 and are omitted.
record.verdict_notes: The reader classed this as T2 'tests' on V4. Under the rules, this is an attack paper reporting its own method's performance against other attacks, so it is T4. All rows are relinked to none and no verdicts are given. If a curator nonetheless wants suffix-ASR evidence for V4, the only defensible reading is narrow. White-box suffixes elicit compliance on 7B open models, with no unattacked baseline reported. Transfer to closed models is low. Table 2's parsed columns are misaligned and must be rechecked against the PDF before any use.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and resulting compliance.
Fine-tuning on benign examples and resulting compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
The study tests optimized adversarial suffix attacks, but not compliant prefilling or decoding changes. It does not isolate whether merely getting past the first response tokens causes the bypass.
Localization of safety behaviour in weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and whether that training holds up.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Individual adversarial-suffix attacks on the four open models in Table 1; MAGIC and several suffix-update methods in Table 3 and Table 4
reader_labels.reason: The reported suffix attacks achieve high ASRs, including 100% in multiple tested settings (r1-r12, r41-r46, r51-r52).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transfer attacks, especially across model families and closed-source targets; also non-saturated individual attack rates
reader_labels.reason: Transfer ASRs vary greatly and are often low or zero; the authors also state transferability may be weaker across model families. Individual attack success is not uniformly near-total (r2, r6, r13-r24, r26-r40, r37-r40, r47-r50).
